rationale: Founders and engineering leads at AI-native SaaS startups — a specific, named role at companies already spending $1k–$10k/month on LLM APIs — are the buyer, and they demonstrably pay for observability tooling (Helicone, Langfuse, Datadog). The $4,200/month real-world story confirms the pain is financially material and the fix is technically tractable: a tagging layer that attributes LLM calls to named features and surfaces a cost breakdown. Buildability is strong because the core is an HTTP proxy/middleware plus a Claude-generated report layer, all achievable without custom ML or compliance work; and once live, delivery, reporting, and billing run automatically with only periodic operator approval gates. All four build gates pass.
solution_plan: LLM Cost Attribution is a hosted micro-service that sits between an AI startup's app and its LLM provider (OpenAI/Anthropic API), tagging every request with a feature name and streaming a daily cost-by-feature report to the founder's inbox. The factory builds it as: a lightweight OpenAI-compatible proxy (a Claude-generated Python script deployed to a free-tier cloud function), a simple sign-up page with Stripe subscription ($49–$149/month), and an intake form collecting the customer's API base-URL and feature tag list — no operator coding. To sell, the factory drafts cold emails targeting AI-native startup founders visible on ProductHunt launches, LinkedIn 'AI startup' filters, and replies in relevant HN threads — each outreach batch is queued for operator approval before sending. Once a customer connects, the proxy runs silently, Claude generates a weekly cost-by-feature digest email automatically, Stripe handles recurring billing, and standard FAQ responses are handled by Claude; the operator's only recurring touch is approving outreach batches and any refund requests. A solo non-technical operator can realistically build and maintain this — the only meaningful risk is that large startups may resist routing production traffic through a third-party proxy, which the validate stage should probe with 3–5 design partners before scaling outreach.
notes: All build gates pass: operational_autonomy=7 (meets min 7), buildability_with_ai=7 (meets min 6), buyer_clarity=8 (meets min 6), willingness_to_pay=8 (meets min 5). Closest competitor gap is feature-level cost attribution specifically, which Helicone and Langfuse do not prioritize. Defensibility grows with per-customer tagging history. Recommended to launch with a design-partner cohort of 3–5 startups before broad outreach.
